clue.text: Take Bill, to church parking by the square

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill to be settled
CE is the Church of England
P is the map and road-sign abbreviation for parking
a T-square is the draughtsman's square, so T stands for it

explanation.surface: Someone is told to take a bill to the church car park beside the town square.
explanation.definitionFit: To take an offer or a gift is to receive it willingly, a plain synonym.

clue.text: A saint as a false model for a Grand Duchess

indicators.note: a false model is a counterfeit version, so the letters are reshaped into another word

explanation.surface: A saint is used as a misleading template for a Russian noblewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false model' tells you to rearrange A SAINT AS A.
explanation.definitionFit: Anastasia was the youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II, subject of famous impostor claims.

clue.text: Military leader and politician come to measure of agreement

parts.note: CO is a commanding officer
MP is a Member of Parliament
an act is a parliamentary measure

explanation.surface: A general and a statesman reach a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'measure of agreement' reads as one phrase, but 'measure' is ACT and 'agreement' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A compact is a formal pact or treaty between parties.

clue.text: It's always so icy-cold in the Underground!

definitions.text: It's always so icy-cold in the Underground!

parts.words: It's always so icy-cold in the Underground!
parts.note: the underground here is the subsoil, which in polar regions stays frozen all year

explanation.surface: A commuter grumbles about the chilly London Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: The Underground suggests the London Tube; the clue means ground that stays frozen beneath the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Permafrost is soil that remains below freezing for years on end, as in the Arctic.

clue.text: How crocodiles travel?

parts.note: a crocodile is also a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs, so the question asks how such a line moves

explanation.surface: A naturalist wonders how the reptiles get about.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'crocodile' is a file of schoolchildren walking two abreast; the reptile is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Children in a crocodile walk in pairs, side by side, like the animals boarding Noah's ark.

clue.text: Checkpoint for vehicles say at Surrey river-crossing?

indicators.note: say signals that the checkpoint's name is pronounced like a place name

parts.note: a weighbridge is a platform where lorries are weighed

explanation.surface: A traveller describes a lorry checkpoint at a bridge in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county south-west of London; Weybridge stands where the River Wey meets the Thames, hence 'river-crossing'.
explanation.definitionFit: The town's name means a bridge over the Wey, a river in the county of Surrey.

clue.text: In Italy singer lacks tone

indicators.note: lacks means the singer's name is missing the word tone

parts.note: a baritone is a male singer
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Italian vocalist has a poor sense of pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a place in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bari is a port city on Italy's Adriatic coast, capital of Apulia.

clue.text: This lance figures, in another Michelangelo work

indicators.note: figures in means appears inside, so the word lies within the following text

explanation.surface: A spear appears among the figures in another Michelangelo painting.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints no comma after 'figures'.
explanation.definitionFit: A thermic lance is a tube of burning iron and oxygen used to cut steel and concrete.

clue.text: The bird on the left's no use!

indicators.note: on in a down clue means the following piece sits beneath, i.e. comes after

parts.note: O is a nought, meaning nothing or no
taken as written
L stands for left

explanation.surface: Someone declares a bird on the left side worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: The ousel is the blackbird, or the related ring ouzel, a member of the thrush family.

clue.text: Combined parties taking care of pound's rise

indicators.note: in a down clue rise means the letters read upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: c/o is short for care of on an envelope
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: An alliance takes charge of a rising currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' turns COLB round to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a coalition of parties or nations acting together.

clue.text: On promotion sailor has given up former vice

definitions.text: On promotion sailor has given up former vice

parts.words: On promotion sailor has given up former vice
parts.note: a naval officer promoted from vice-... drops the word vice from his rank

explanation.surface: A sailor who has risen in rank claims to have abandoned his old bad habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' looks like a moral failing, but it is the rank prefix of a vice-admiral, whose next step up removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank above vice-admiral is the full flag rank, the top naval officer title.

clue.text: City-dwellers often bold in speech?

explanation.surface: Urban residents are said to be outspoken.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a yorker is a ball pitched at the batsman's feet that often gets him out: 'bold in speech' sounds like 'bowled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of York are its citizens; and the cricket delivery of that name frequently has batsmen bowled, which 'bold' sounds like.

clue.text: Right to a cavern perhaps in an old Indian state

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters given could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A traveller heads right towards a cave somewhere in a former Indian princely state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals rearranging R plus TOACAVERN.
explanation.definitionFit: Travancore was a princely state in the far south of British India, now part of Kerala.

clue.text: German boy bearing coin from Cyprus

parts.note: a compass bearing such as east gives E
the mil was a small coin of Cyprus under British rule

explanation.surface: A German lad carries a coin from Cyprus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' looks like 'carrying' but is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Emil is a common German masculine first name, as in the children's book Emil and the Detectives.

clue.text: With aid of a coin perhaps we get a fan

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters given could form something else

explanation.surface: Someone becomes a supporter with the help of a coin toss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals rearranging AIDOFACOIN.
explanation.definitionFit: An aficionado is a keen enthusiast or devotee, originally of bullfighting.

clue.text: Like Juvenal's work — or old Greek drama, say?

indicators.note: say tells the solver to pronounce the word for the drama and hear another

parts.note: the satyric drama was the bawdy satyr play of ancient Athens

explanation.surface: A classicist asks whether Juvenal's poems resemble Greek drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Juvenal was a Roman poet famous for his biting verse satires.

clue.text: A summons — sort of lousy …unfeeling way to treat us

parts.note: a call is a summons

indicators.note: sort of means a version of the word lousy, its letters reordered

explanation.surface: Someone complains that being summoned was a lousy and heartless way to treat them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' turns LOUSY into OUSLY.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat someone callously is to act with hard-hearted indifference.

clue.text: Actually it may not be legal

explanation.surface: Someone admits that something is not strictly lawful.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase for 'in fact' contrasts with de jure, 'by law', so an arrangement existing in fact may lack legal sanction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag means in reality; and a state of affairs existing in practice rather than by right may not be lawful.

clue.text: Dressed to go in for dinner?

definitions.text: Dressed to go in for dinner?

parts.words: Dressed to go in for dinner?
parts.note: a dressed bird is plucked and trussed, ready to be put in the cooker for a meal

explanation.surface: A guest is dressed and ready to enter the dining room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed' and 'go in for dinner' suggest a diner in evening wear; it means poultry prepared for roasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Food sold prepared and needing only to be cooked is so described.

clue.text: Spray a damaged rose and see a return

indicators.note: damaged means the word rose is broken up and its letters reordered
a return asks for the short word for see to be read backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning see or behold

explanation.surface: A gardener sprays a ruined rose and watches it recover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spray' could be a bunch of flowers to go with the rose, but it is the definition; 'damaged' is the anagram signal and 'a return' reverses the archaic word for see.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerosol is a pressurised can that releases its contents as a fine mist.

clue.text: Break promise to M. Clair and guest? No way!

parts.note: René Clair was a French film director, Monsieur Clair

indicators.note: No means the short word for way is left out of guest

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A host breaks a promise to the French director and his guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No way' looks like a refusal; ST (street) is taken from GUEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To renegue (more often renege) is to go back on one's word.

clue.text: Fence in French playing-field

parts.note: en is the French word for in
a close is an ... field, used for school games

explanation.surface: A fence is put round a French sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fence in' reads as the definition, but 'in' belongs with 'French'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fence land is to shut it in with a barrier.

clue.text: The detachment's not in position

parts.note: out is the opposite of in
a post is a position or job

explanation.surface: A military unit is away from its station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The detachment's' means 'the detachment is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a small military station or unit set apart from the main force.

clue.text: In Scotland go for the workers' group

explanation.surface: A Scot sets off to join a team of labourers.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots dialect uses this verb to mean walk or go; and a crew of labourers working together is the same word.

clue.text: General assignment

explanation.surface: A senior officer gets a new posting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses S. Grant was the Union commander in the American Civil War; and an allocation of funds or land is also so called.

clue.text: Composer gives the old king a drink

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry monarch of the nursery rhyme
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A musician hands an elderly monarch a glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Cole Porter was the American songwriter of Anything Goes and Night and Day.

clue.text: See opening for estate agent

indicators.note: opening for means the first letter of the word estate

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

explanation.surface: An estate agent has an opening to see.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of, an old literary synonym.

clue.text: Smelly old one perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps here loosely invites the solver to fit one letter into the word old

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Something old, perhaps, gives off a bad odour.
explanation.walkthrough: The container signal is loose: the I (one) goes inside OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Olid is a rare word for foul-smelling or fetid.

clue.text: Millet production once meant a bit of money to us

parts.note: the angel was an old English gold coin
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painting by Millet once earned some cash for the speaker's family.
explanation.walkthrough: Millet is the French painter, not the grain; The Angelus shows two peasants praying in a field.
explanation.definitionFit: The Angelus is Jean-François Millet's famous canvas of peasants pausing to pray at dusk.

clue.text: Player giving a sound but mechanical performance

definitions.text: Player giving a sound but mechanical performance

parts.words: Player giving a sound but mechanical performance
parts.note: a player piano plays soundly but by machinery, not by a human performer

explanation.surface: A musician plays competently but without feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a person; it is the player piano, whose 'mechanical performance' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pianola is a self-playing piano driven by perforated paper rolls.

clue.text: Producers of graceful children

parts.note: the nursery rhyme says a child born on a certain weekday is full of grace

explanation.surface: Parents are praised for raising elegant offspring.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' continues 'Tuesday's child is full of grace'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old rhyme about birth weekdays, those born on the third day of the week are blessed with grace.

clue.text: Stout or wine left to head of YMCA

parts.note: port is a fortified wine

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the word YMCA

explanation.surface: Someone chooses between beer and wine at the YMCA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like a beer to go with 'wine' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout describes a heavily built person, rotund and well-fed.
